tip: fy (my) triggers a nasal change: coesau turns into fy nghoesau (my legs), c becoming ngh.
After fy (my) the next word nasal-mutates: tad becomes fy nhad-cu here, t shifting to nh.
fy (my) turns b into m: braich becomes fy mraich (my arm).
The -odd ending marks a he/she past tense: hedfan (to fly) becomes Hedfanodd (flew).
drwy (through) softens the next word: Cymru becomes drwy Gymru, c changing to g.
Add -ach to an adjective for the comparative: dwfn (deep) gives the ddyfnach here (deeper).
am before a verb-noun means 'want to' or 'intend to': am rannu here is 'want to share'.
Front the subject and add a for emphasis: Fy nhad a ddysgodd = it was my father who taught.
ces i is the past of cael (to get): ces i'r llythyr = I got the letter.
Adjectives can take a plural form beside plural nouns: cryf (strong) becomes cryfion for gwyntoedd.
Roedd plus a verb-noun means 'used to': Roedd e bob amser yn darllen = he used to read.
Byddwn i means 'I would', the conditional of bod: Byddwn i wrth fy modd = I'd love it.
Modern Welsh counts in tens: naw deg pump is nine-ten-five, that is ninety-five.
Month names take mis in front: mis Mehefin is literally 'month of June'.
Welsh often drops 'that' in relative clauses: Dyna'r tŷ adeiladodd fy nhad-cu = the house my grandfather built.
gwaethaf means 'worst', an irregular superlative of drwg (bad); it appears here as waethaf.
chi is the polite or plural 'you'; ti is for friends and children.
lle means 'where', linking a place to what happens in it: yr afon lle mae'r eogiaid yn silio.
yn before a verb-noun makes an ongoing action: mae'r plant yn adeiladu = the children are building.
o (from) softens the next word: patrymau becomes o batrymau, p changing to b.
yw links two nouns as equal: Bangor yw'r ddinas hynaf = Bangor is the oldest city.
debyg (similar) is followed by i for 'to': debyg i fy nhad = similar to my father.
a (and) triggers an aspirate change: cerddoriaeth becomes a cherddoriaeth, c turning to ch.
wedi plus a verb-noun makes the perfect: Dw i wedi brifo = I have hurt.
After yn a noun softens its first letter: bardd (poet) becomes yn fardd here.
Rwy'n is a common 'I am', short for Rydw i yn: Rwy'n falch = I'm proud.
ar ôl (after) is followed by a verb-noun: ar ôl gweithio = after working.
